title: Air India Launches Restaurant-Style Fine Dining in Business Class
excerpt: The course-by-course service, with linen tables and bespoke Vista Verve tableware, has launched on India-UK routes and will expand across the A350, 787-9 and 777-300 fleets.
body:
• Air India announced on October 22 a restaurant-style, course-by-course fine dining service for Business Class on select long-haul and ultra-long-haul flights.
  • It has launched on India-UK routes serving London Heathrow, London Gatwick and Birmingham, replacing the single tray with linen-laid tables and individually plated appetisers, mains and desserts.
  • The service will expand progressively across Airbus A350, Boeing 787-9 and Boeing 777-300 aircraft - check your specific flight, as rollout is phased, not network-wide on day one.
  • A new Vista Verve tableware collection includes dedicated plates for each course, signature glassware, an espresso cup and a Martaban-inspired cruet set.

Air India has replaced the Business Class meal tray with a restaurant sequence on its longest flights. Announced on October 22, the new service serves appetisers, main courses and desserts separately, each individually plated, on linen-covered tables with dedicated tableware. It has launched on flights between India and the United Kingdom - London Heathrow, London Gatwick and Birmingham - and will expand progressively across the airline's Airbus A350, Boeing 787-9 and Boeing 777-300 fleets, according to Outlook Traveller and PAX International.

"At Air India, we are continually reimagining every aspect of the customer experience. The introduction of our fine dining-style, course-by-course meal service in Business Class is another step in our broader Air India transformation journey."

- Rajesh Dogra, Chief Customer Experience Officer, Air India

What changes at the seat

The change is in presentation and pacing, not only in the menu. Instead of every component arriving together, cabin crew serve each course in turn, which lets passengers eat at a more leisurely pace and gives crew more scope to personalise the service. The tableware is part of the product: the Vista Verve collection includes dedicated plates for appetisers, main courses, snacks, desserts and cheese, signature glassware and a specially designed espresso cup. Its centrepiece is a Martaban-inspired cruet set, drawn from the traditional Indian jars used to store ingredients and preserve flavours and family recipes, a detail both Outlook Traveller and PAX International reported in their coverage of the launch.

The food and the London catering switch

Live From A Lounge, which covered the launch in detail, noted that Air India has also moved its London catering to DO & CO, the premium flight caterer at Heathrow and Gatwick, alongside the new cutlery and dining flow on ex-London flights. The site described a broader dining overhaul already under way: a refreshed global menu combining regional Indian dishes with international options, including Awadhi-inspired vegetarian and non-vegetarian meals, Japanese Teppanyaki bowls and chicken bibimbap, plus expanded home-style, plant-based and special-dietary options and work on the wine programme. Read its full account of the London catering switch for the route-level detail.

Why the UK came first

The United Kingdom is one of Air India's most important long-haul markets and one where it competes directly for premium passengers against carriers that have sold restaurant-style dining for years. Singapore Airlines' Book the Cook, cited by Live From A Lounge as a benchmark, lets eligible passengers choose from an expanded menu before departure. Air India's test is different and harder to fake: consistency. A multi-course service takes more crew time and coordination than a tray, must be balanced against sleep on overnight flights, and has to taste as good as it photographs after food prepared in advance is loaded, chilled and reheated in a galley.

What this means for diaspora travellers

For readers flying Business Class between India and the UK - and, as the rollout reaches the A350, 787-9 and 777-300 fleets, on other long-haul and ultra-long-haul routes - the practical step is to check the aircraft and route on your booking before assuming the new service is aboard. The launch is phased by route and aircraft, not a single fleet-wide switch, and Air India has not published a flight-by-flight completion schedule.

What happens next

Air India says the service will extend to additional international routes over time, building on refreshed menus, an award-winning wine selection and upgraded tea offerings, alongside new A350 and 787-9 aircraft and cabin retrofits. Whether course-by-course dining becomes a reason to choose Air India over rivals will be decided by passengers on the expanded routes - and by whether the first UK flights deliver the same standard on a Tuesday in February as they did at launch.
